Adapting DietView to your own survey

Source: vignettes/articles/extending.Rmd
extending.Rmd

DietView makes few assumptions about your data: one row per prey record, a predator column, a stomach column and a prey key. Everything else is declared. This article goes through the choices you make when you move from the example table to your own survey, in the order you meet them.

library(DietView)

1. Map your columns

Tell dv_spec() which of your columns plays which role. Your table keeps its own column names:

spec <- dv_spec(predator = "sp", stomach = "stom", prey_id = "aphia",
                prey_name = "prey", weight = "wt_g", digestion = "dig",
                covariates = c("yr", "zone"))
dv_validate(mydata, spec)

Two columns need care. The stomach identifier must be unique across the whole table, not only within a predator or a year: stomach counts (frequency of occurrence, aggregation thresholds, matrices) count distinct identifiers, so two stomachs that share an identifier count as one. If your identifiers restart each year, build a unique one first, for example mydata$stom <- paste(mydata$year, mydata$sp, mydata$stom_no, sep = "_"). And give both a prey ID and a prey name when you have them: the ID is used for the lookup, and the name lets DietView check that the two agree.

2. Attach a taxonomy you can check

With taxonomy = "worms", DietView looks each distinct prey up in the World Register of Marine Species and keeps a log of how it was matched. Read that log before you use the result:

prep <- dv_prepare(mydata, spec, taxonomy = "worms")
dv_taxonomy_report(prep)   # the matches that need a look, largest first

Each prey gets a match_type:

match_type Meaning What to do
id The AphiaID is accepted in WoRMS Nothing, unless name_check is "differs"
id_synonym The AphiaID is unaccepted; its accepted ID was used Check that the accepted name is the taxon you meant
id_unchecked WoRMS could not be reached to check the ID Run again later
exact No ID; the name matched exactly Nothing
fuzzy No ID; the name was matched by TAXAMATCH, which tolerates misspellings Check every one: a near match can be a different taxon
unresolved No match Correct the name, or accept that the prey stays unidentified

A name_check of "differs" means the name in your table is not the name WoRMS holds for that AphiaID: either the ID or the name was mistyped. A lineage_ok of FALSE means the prey was matched but its classification could not be retrieved; its records count as unidentified until you run the lookup again. Fix what the report lists, then save the lineage.

3. Freeze the taxonomy for the analysis

WoRMS changes. For an analysis you will publish, resolve the taxonomy once, save it as a lineage table, and run every later step from that file:

lineage <- unique(prep$data[, c(spec$prey_name, prep$ranks)])
write.csv(lineage, "lineage_2026-10-20.csv", row.names = FALSE)

lineage <- read.csv("lineage_2026-10-20.csv", na.strings = c("NA", ""))
prep <- dv_prepare(mydata, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = lineage)

This path needs neither worrms nor a network connection, and it gives the same result every time it is run on the same files. Archive the lineage table with your data and record the date it was retrieved. The lineage table needs one row per prey key, with one column per rank; an empty cell means the prey was not identified to that rank. A prey that is missing from the lineage table, or a key that appears twice, triggers a warning or an error instead of passing unnoticed.

If you build the lineage table by hand, for example for prey outside WoRMS, take the classification from one stated authority and cite it.

4. Choose the ranks

By default DietView shows seven ranks, kingdom to species. Pass ranks to show others:

spec <- dv_spec(predator = "sp", stomach = "stom", prey_name = "prey",
                ranks = c("phylum", "class", "order", "family", "genus"))

Rank names are WoRMS rank names in lower case, so intermediate ranks such as "subclass" or "infraclass" can be added on the WoRMS path. With a lineage table, every rank you list must be a column of that table.

Fewer ranks make a simpler figure, but they also merge information: without "species", a prey named to species and one named only to its genus look the same. Check one more thing on your own prey list: some taxa have no entry at one of the requested ranks in WoRMS. Such a prey shows an unidentified node at that rank with named taxa beyond it, and that node then mixes prey that were not identified with prey that were identified but have no taxon at that rank. Inspect the rows of dv_rank_table() labeled NA that have children before you report an unidentified share at that rank.

5. Colors

dv_palette() gives each name a color and unidentified nodes white. Build it from the names in your own data rather than typing them:

lin <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "dietview_example_lineage.csv", package = "DietView"),
                na.strings = c("NA", ""))
pal <- dv_palette(lin$class)
pal
#> Malacostraca    Teleostei     Bivalvia   Polychaeta     Copepoda           NA 
#>    "#1f77b4"    "#aec7e8"    "#ff7f0e"    "#ffbb78"    "#2ca02c"    "#FFFFFF"

Pass the result to dv_sunburst(colors = pal). To give one taxon a color of your choice, change that element: pal[["Malacostraca"]] <- "#1f77b4". The palette has 20 colors and reuses them after that.

6. Periods and length classes

Add a covariate column, list it in dv_spec(covariates = ), and build periods and length bins with the helpers:

dv_add_period(c(2005, 2010, 2012, 2019), breaks = c(2003, 2010, 2020))
#> [1] 2003-2010 2003-2010 2011-2020 2011-2020
#> Levels: 2003-2010 2011-2020
dv_size_bins(c(22, 30, 41, 58), breaks = c(0, 30, 45, 60))
#> [1] [0, 30)  [30, 45) [30, 45) [45, 60)
#> Levels: [0, 30) [30, 45) [45, 60)

A year on an inner break goes to the earlier period (2010 above), and a length on an inner break goes to the bin that starts there (30 cm above). Values outside the breaks get no level. The article on covariates shows how to compare diets across the levels.

7. Freshwater, terrestrial and mixed prey

WoRMS covers marine taxa and many brackish and freshwater ones. When DietView matches a name without an ID, it restricts the search to marine records, so a strictly freshwater or terrestrial prey named without an AphiaID will often be unresolved. For such prey, build a lineage table from an authority that covers them (for example GBIF or the Catalogue of Life) and use taxonomy = "table" (section 3). If your prey list mixes marine and other taxa, resolve the marine part with WoRMS, append the rest by hand from the other authority, and say in your methods which authority supplied which part.
